newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia retail weakness reflects soft job market.
newsitem.headline: Australia retail weakness reflects soft job market.

text.p: Ongoing weakness in Australia's retail sector is a reflection of the stagnant labour market, analysts said, adding that June retail data justified the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) rate cut on Wednesday.
With unemployment stalled above 8.5 percent, not only was there no new spending being generated from employment growth, but the confidence of those with jobs was also affected.
Retail trade fell 1.8 percent in June, against expectations of a 0.4 percent rise, official figures on Thursday showed. It was the third fall in the past four months.
"The weakness in employment means that the momentum for additional retail spending is not coming through," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
"If you don't have a job, you don't earn money; if you don't earn money, you can't spend any money," he said.

Over the June quarter, real retail trade -- which adjusts nominal retail trade for price effects -- fell 0.5 percent, implying a soft contribution to June quarter gross domestic product. Forecasts had centred on a 0.1 percent rise.

"The latest data confirms continuing soft underlying consumer spending activity in recent months, with continuing weak labour market conditions dampening consumer confidence and spending," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
Within the overall fall, the weakest sector was department store retailing which fell 10.5 percent in the month and was down 7.2 percent in real terms over the quarter.

Economists suggested this may be due to seasonal factors with some clearance sales being held over until July from June. Some of the fall was also seen as a correction to the strong 2.9 percent rise in May.
Peters said the data highlighted why the RBA had moved to cut the official cash rate to 5.0 percent from 5.5 percent on Wednesday.
It was the fifth cut of 50 basis points in the past year, in a move intended to help the economy grow faster and generate employment growth.
"The numbers are very weak and they do justify the Reserve Bank's actions (on Wednesday)," ANZ Treasury senior economist David De Garis said.
After that cut, attention turned to the possibility of a sixth cut in rates being delivered, but that was generally seen as not likely in the near term.
"These are the sort of numbers the market would see as pushing towards an easing, but not for the next three or four months at least, I wouldn't think," De Garis said.

While a sixth cut remained only speculation at this stage, analysts said the market's bias would remain on the side of an easing, until there were signs that the impact of the five cuts was starting to feed through to the economy.
The poor retail figures were good news for debt markets, with the 10-year bond futures contract surging to an all-time high, and bill futures moving to under the official cash rate.

Shortly after the data was released, the September 10-year contract rose to a record 93.650, and posted further gains to reach a high of 93.670. December 90-day bill futures rose to a high of 95.14, an implied yield of 4.86 percent.
"They (the market) know that rates aren't going to go up in the next six to nine months, so the opposite bet is they may go down," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
